questions.stem: What does a security group do in an Amazon VPC?

options.text: Acts as a virtual firewall for instances
options.rationale: Security groups control inbound and outbound traffic for the resources they are associated with.

options.text: Encrypts data stored on Amazon EBS volumes
options.rationale: Encryption at rest is a storage feature, not a security group function.

options.text: Gives a set of IAM users the same permissions
options.rationale: That is an IAM group.

options.text: Scans instances for malware and vulnerabilities
options.rationale: Vulnerability scanning is done by Amazon Inspector.

questions.explanation: Security groups work at the instance (network interface) level; network ACLs work at the subnet level.

questions.stem: Which statement about security groups and network ACLs is correct?

options.text: Security groups are stateless; network ACLs are stateful
options.rationale: This reverses the two.

options.text: Security groups are stateful; network ACLs are stateless
options.rationale: Return traffic is automatically allowed by a security group, but a network ACL evaluates each direction separately.

options.text: Both are applied at the subnet level
options.rationale: Security groups apply to instances; network ACLs apply to subnets.

options.text: Network ACLs cannot contain deny rules
options.rationale: Network ACLs support both allow and deny rules.

questions.explanation: Security groups support allow rules only and are stateful. Network ACLs support allow and deny rules and are stateless.

questions.stem: At which level does a network ACL control traffic in an Amazon VPC?

options.rationale: Instance-level filtering is done by security groups; mixing the two up is the most common mistake.
A network ACL is created in a VPC, but it is associated with subnets and checks traffic at each subnet's edge.
A network ACL allows or denies traffic as it enters or leaves a subnet.
Network ACLs belong to a VPC and apply to subnets, not whole Regions.

questions.explanation: A network ACL checks traffic as it enters or leaves a subnet, so one ACL covers every instance in the subnets it is associated with. A security group is attached to each instance instead, so remember: ACL = subnet, security group = instance.

questions.stem: Which service protects web applications from common exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting?

options.rationale: Shield focuses on DDoS protection.
GuardDuty detects threats from account and network activity.
Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities.
AWS WAF is a web application firewall that filters HTTP and HTTPS requests based on rules.

questions.explanation: AWS WAF protects at the application layer with rules for common attack patterns; Shield protects against DDoS.

questions.stem: Where can a company find and buy third-party security software, such as firewalls and endpoint protection, that runs on AWS?

options.rationale: AWS Marketplace is a catalog of third-party software, including security products.
Artifact provides compliance reports.
Security Hub aggregates findings; it is not a software store.
Trusted Advisor checks your account against best practices.

questions.explanation: AWS Marketplace offers third-party security solutions from AWS Partners that integrate with AWS services.

questions.stem: Which service can check an AWS account for security issues such as security groups with unrestricted ports or a root user without MFA?

options.rationale: IAM is where you set up MFA and permissions, but it does not scan the account for issues such as open security group ports.
Trusted Advisor security checks include security groups with unrestricted ports and MFA on the root account.
Inspector scans workloads for software vulnerabilities, not account settings like root MFA.
Shield protects against DDoS attacks.

questions.explanation: The clue is account-wide best-practice checks such as open ports and root user MFA: Trusted Advisor runs these security checks. Inspector scans workloads for software vulnerabilities rather than checking account settings.

questions.stem: Where can a customer find articles answering common AWS questions, written by AWS Support engineers?

options.rationale: Artifact provides compliance reports.
Marketplace is a software catalog.
The Knowledge Center, part of AWS re:Post, answers frequently asked questions from AWS customers.
Prescriptive Guidance offers guides and patterns from AWS experts for cloud projects, not answers to common support questions.

questions.explanation: The clue is short answers to common questions from AWS Support: the Knowledge Center on AWS re:Post. Prescriptive Guidance is longer planning and implementation guidance for cloud adoption projects.

questions.stem: Where would a customer read posts by AWS security experts about new security features and best practices?

options.rationale: Artifact provides compliance reports and agreements.
Cost Explorer analyzes spending.
AWS Config records resource configurations.
The AWS Security Blog publishes security guidance, announcements and how-to posts.

questions.explanation: The AWS Security Blog is one of the main sources of security information, along with the Knowledge Center and the AWS security website.

questions.stem: By default, which traffic does a newly created security group allow?

options.text: Outbound traffic, but no inbound traffic
options.rationale: A new security group has no inbound rules and one outbound rule that allows all traffic.

options.text: All inbound traffic and all outbound traffic
options.rationale: Inbound traffic is denied until you add rules.

options.text: No inbound and no outbound traffic
options.rationale: Outbound traffic is allowed by default.

options.text: Inbound web traffic on port 80 alone
options.rationale: No inbound rules exist by default.

questions.explanation: Security groups deny inbound traffic unless a rule allows it, which is why you add rules for the ports your application needs.

questions.stem: Which TWO can be used to control network traffic in an Amazon VPC? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: Cost Explorer analyzes spending.
Network ACLs filter traffic for subnets.
Artifact provides compliance reports.
Security groups filter traffic for instances and other resources.
Password policies apply to IAM user sign-in, not network traffic.

questions.explanation: Security groups and network ACLs are the two VPC traffic controls; using both adds defense in depth.

questions.stem: AWS WAF can protect a website when it is deployed with which service?

options.rationale: EBS is block storage.
AWS WAF can protect resources such as CloudFront distributions, API Gateway REST APIs and AWS Amplify apps.
Glacier is archival storage.
AWS Backup manages backups.

questions.explanation: AWS WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests at the services that front your application.

questions.stem: Which kinds of rules can a security group contain?

options.text: Deny rules, with no allow rules
options.rationale: Security groups do not support deny rules.
That describes network ACLs.

options.text: Allow rules, with no deny rules
options.rationale: Security groups support allow rules; traffic not allowed is denied.

options.text: Rules based on IAM user names
options.rationale: Security groups filter by protocol, port and source, not by IAM user.

questions.explanation: Use network ACLs when you need explicit deny rules.

questions.stem: Which offering adds 24/7 access to the AWS Shield Response Team and protection against DDoS-related scaling charges?

options.rationale: Shield Advanced adds expert response support and cost protection for DDoS-related scaling.
Shield Standard is automatic, basic protection without these extras.
AWS WAF filters web requests.
GuardDuty detects threats.

questions.explanation: Shield Standard is included for everyone; Shield Advanced is a paid upgrade.

questions.stem: Where can a customer find AWS security bulletins about newly discovered vulnerabilities and how they affect AWS services?

options.rationale: Artifact provides AWS compliance reports and agreements, not vulnerability notices.

options.text: On the AWS security bulletins page
options.rationale: AWS publishes security bulletins for reported vulnerabilities that affect its services.

options.text: In AWS Trusted Advisor security checks
options.rationale: Trusted Advisor checks your own account against best practices.
The Health Dashboard reports service events and changes that affect your AWS resources.

questions.explanation: The clue is public notices about newly found vulnerabilities, often with CVE numbers: AWS publishes these as security bulletins on its security website. Artifact holds compliance reports, not vulnerability notices.

questions.stem: A company uses security groups and network ACLs together for the same workload. Which security principle does this follow?

options.rationale: Elasticity is about scaling capacity.
Economies of scale are about pricing.
Several independent layers of control mean one mistake does not expose the workload.
Data sovereignty is about where data lives.

questions.explanation: The clue is two independent controls on one workload: layering subnet-level network ACLs with instance-level security groups is defense in depth, so a single misconfiguration does not expose the workload.

questions.stem: Which VPC feature captures information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces, which is useful for security analysis?

options.rationale: CloudTrail records API calls, not network traffic.
AWS Config records configuration changes.
Artifact provides compliance reports.
Flow logs record accepted and rejected traffic metadata for network interfaces.

questions.explanation: Flow logs can be published to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3.

questions.stem: Which TWO filter network or web traffic on AWS? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3.
AWS WAF filters web requests.
Artifact provides compliance reports.
Budgets tracks spending.
Network ACLs filter subnet traffic.

questions.explanation: AWS WAF filters web (HTTP and HTTPS) requests, and network ACLs filter traffic entering or leaving subnets. Macie, Artifact and Budgets do not filter traffic.

questions.stem: A company wants to be alerted if one of its Amazon EC2 instances starts communicating with IP addresses known to be malicious. Which service should it turn on?

options.rationale: Inspector scans workloads for software vulnerabilities and network exposure; it does not watch for malicious activity.
GuardDuty uses threat intelligence, such as lists of malicious IP addresses, to detect suspicious activity in the account.
AWS WAF filters incoming web requests to applications; it does not alert on an instance's outbound connections.
Shield Advanced adds DDoS protection and response support.

questions.explanation: The clue is suspicious activity that is already happening, checked against known malicious IP addresses: GuardDuty is the threat detection service. Inspector is the nearest neighbor, but it looks for vulnerabilities that could be exploited rather than active threats.

questions.stem: A company needs to block all traffic from one specific IP address to every instance in a subnet. Which VPC feature can do this?

options.rationale: Security groups support allow rules but not deny rules, so they cannot block one address.
Route tables direct traffic to targets such as gateways; they do not filter traffic by source.
Network ACLs support deny rules and apply to all traffic entering or leaving a subnet.
Flow logs record information about traffic but do not block it.

questions.explanation: Two clues point to a network ACL: the rule must deny a specific address, and it must cover a whole subnet. Security groups are the nearest neighbor, but they are attached to individual resources and can only allow traffic.
